description: We are a group named The Forest - we are working on the Interplanetary Survival Guide - Mars challenge. Our team has methods from astrophysics, AI/ML, computer hardware and data analytics. Our goal is to make a system that uses data to help people survive when they explore Mars. We need other individuals to work with us who have skills in writing code, making data charts and studying planets but also speaking or writing clearly.
summary: Marswalk Planner is a multi-layer web map that helps a suited astronaut plan a safe Marswalk in Jezero Crater, built for the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge. It combines NASA Mars Trek imagery (CTX mosaic), MOLA relief and a slope grid built from the USGS MOLA–HRSC blended DEM (NASA MOLA and ESA HRSC, 200 m/pixel). The user picks a habitat and a target, and a Dijkstra engine returns fast, safe and science routes, with the walk-back time computed at every point. The key output is the Point of No Return (PNR): the point after which a safe return is no longer guaranteed given the EVA budget, a 60-minute oxygen reserve and, in crisis mode, an incoming dust storm. It is drawn as an uncertainty band, so the astronaut sees how far is too far. An offline, rule-based helmet assistant, designed for the 4–24 minute Earth–Mars signal delay, recommends continue, shorten or return. Thresholds come from NASA’s EVA Concept of Operations (20° slope limit, 6 ± 2 h EVA, about 2 km/h), and every value is labeled NASA, analog or team assumption.
details:
What it does and how it works. The map shows Mars Trek CTX imagery, MOLA shaded relief and a slope overlay. A min-heap Dijkstra engine (8 neighbors, no diagonal corner-cutting) builds three routes: fast, safe and science. Walking speed follows v = vmax·exp(−3.5·tan θ), with vmax = 2 km/h, NASA’s planning value for flat regolith; the exponential form is adapted from Tobler’s walking function and is a team assumption. Slope is graded in four tiers: below 5.7° comfortable (team assumption), 5.7°–17° slowing (analog test range), 17°–20° high risk (NASA) and above 20° impassable (NASA). A reverse Dijkstra from the habitat gives the walk-back time to every cell. At each route point, slack = budget − (elapsed + walk-back) − safety margin, where budget = min(EVA time, time to storm). The 60-minute margin is NASA’s backup-oxygen hour treated as a reserve (team decision). The PNR is the first point where slack turns negative, drawn as a band between 1.15× and 0.80× speed factors (team assumption). The EVA budget is 360 minutes (NASA’s 6 h plan); the demo can be run at 240 minutes, the low end of NASA’s 6 ± 2 h range.

Science route. Cells are scored 0–1 by a team-defined criterion: how strongly orbital CRISM indicators suggest past water and habitability. Phyllosilicates (Fe/Mg-smectite) score 0.90–1.00, carbonates (Mg-carbonate) 0.75–0.85, and sulfates and other hydrated salts 0.55–0.70, with weight b = 0.6 so route cost never turns negative. CRISM summary products show spectral feature strength, not mineral abundance, so we treat the map as a detection indicator. Cells outside CRISM coverage are marked “No Data” (score 0), are not interpolated, and are crossed at normal cost.

Crisis mode and helmet assistant. At about 6 mbar, wind force on an astronaut is negligible even in strong dust storms, so we do not model it. Storms act through dust opacity: τ from 1 to 5 maps to a walking-speed factor from 1.0 to 0.45 (team assumption). The scenario is a replay-style simulation based on the 2018 global dust storm and always shows the label “SIMULATION: replay of a past dust storm. There is no real-time weather data from Mars.” The helmet assistant runs fully offline on the device, because Earth–Mars signal delay is 4–24 minutes. It is a deterministic, rule-based risk score with hand-set weights and uses no machine learning.

Impact. Mission planners get one explainable answer to “how far can we go and still get home?”, and astronaut trainers get a simple way to teach return-time discipline. The PNR depends on the EVA budget, so the tool shows plainly that some walks are not feasible: on a 40 km area, two points 20 km apart with a 240-minute EVA are mostly beyond the PNR. This is not a bug; it shows that crossing the crater on foot is out of reach. Every recommendation traces back to its inputs.

Creativity. Most route tools minimize distance or effort. Marswalk Planner makes the return, not the outbound trip, the primary quantity, and shows its uncertainty as a band. Every parameter carries a provenance label (NASA, analog, team assumption), and the tool refuses to guess where data is missing.

Validity. The route engine has unit tests that check physical expectations: on flat ground, time equals distance over speed; the PNR falls near (budget − margin)/2 (for a 240-minute budget, 60-minute margin and 2 km/h, about 90 minutes and 3 km from the habitat); the PNR moves toward the habitat as the budget shrinks; reverse Dijkstra equals forward Dijkstra; and the JSON output arrays are complete and consistent. The thresholds come from NASA’s EVA Concept of Operations and the EVA Walkback Test report, and the team’s own decisions are listed separately.

Tools and data. JavaScript (DOM-free engine, unit-tested in Node), HTML5 Canvas, OpenLayers 9.2.4, NASA Mars Trek WMTS layers (CTX 5 m source mosaic, MOLA), Python with NumPy and Rasterio/GDAL for DEM cropping and the slope grid, and a JSON data contract between components. Elevation: USGS MOLA–HRSC blended DEM v2 (200 m/pixel), combining NASA MGS MOLA and ESA Mars Express HRSC. Mineral references: MRO CRISM. Reference: ESA/FU Berlin interactive Jezero map.

Limitations (stated openly). NASA lists Mars walking ranges and the Mars suit as future work; most of our walking and oxygen numbers come from Moon-gravity and 1-g analog tests, and Mars gravity makes suited walking harder, so they may be optimistic. The 20° limit is a lunar suit (xEMU) requirement. Slope is computed without direction, so uphill and downhill take equal time, which underestimates uphill cost. A 200 m DEM describes regional terrain, not rocks or pits at walking-step scale; the USGS blend is an interim product and HRSC covers only part of Mars. Curiosity RAD and Perseverance MEDA data are single-station measurements, not a surface-wide layer, and are not part of route cost. The tool is an educational and mission-planning concept, not an operational decision aid.
